notes.title: Start here: OpsForge and its two study tracks
notes.body:
This repo is OpsForge, a training codebase for an internal operations console (Next.js, Auth.js, Drizzle, BullMQ). It has two study tracks: `fable-docs/`, nine chapters that tell the story of the system, and `_learning/guides/`, one guide per source file.

This quest uses:

1. `fable-docs/04-authentication.md`: sign-in, roles and permissions.
2. `fable-docs/07-operations-engine.md`: the pipeline for dangerous actions.
3. `fable-docs/08-domain-services.md`: feature flags, incident severity and the audit log.
4. `_learning/guides/root/middleware.guide.md`: the request gate in `middleware.ts`.

Many function bodies in this repo are deliberate stubs, and the chapters say so. The few real functions are short, so you can evaluate them by hand: pick inputs at and around every threshold, and walk each branch. The quiz asks you to predict exact return values, so do that with a pencil before answering.

readMore.why: The map of all nine chapters and how they connect.

notes.title: Concept: policy as code, roles as data
notes.body:
Two small files decide who may do what.

**Roles as data.** `src/lib/auth/rbac.ts` holds a `rolePermissions` table: one array of permission keys per role. `hasPermission` is a lookup in that table. Copy the table into a grid (roles down, permissions across) and tick each cell; that grid answers most role questions faster than re-reading the file. Then read the last line of `hasPermission` and ask what happens for a role string that is not a key of the table.

**Policy as code.** `src/lib/approvals/policies.ts` is one boolean expression. Chapter 7's Exercise 2 asks you to probe it. Before reading the chapter's hint, list the two conditions, decide the exact boundary of the numeric one (is it inclusive?), and test it against a few command keys from `src/lib/operations/commands/` and a few you invent.

Finally read `src/lib/operations/commands/registry.ts` and search the repo for the places that call each of its two functions.

excerpts.quote: With RBAC, that change is *one line in one file*.

notes.title: Concept: classifiers, buckets and rule engines
notes.body:
Chapter 8 covers the real algorithms in the codebase. Each is a few lines long.

- **A classifier** (`src/lib/incidents/severity.ts`) turns a continuous error rate into a category through ordered threshold checks. Note the comparison operator used for each threshold, then evaluate the function at each threshold value exactly.
- **Bucketing** (`src/lib/feature-flags/rollout.ts`) hashes a flag key and a customer id to a number. Work out the range of numbers it can return, then read how `evaluateFlag` compares that number with `rolloutPercentage`, and try the extreme percentages.
- **A rule engine** (`evaluateFlag` in `src/lib/feature-flags/evaluator.ts`) combines targeting rules. Read the guard clauses at the top first. Then look at how the rules array is combined and how the conditions inside one rule are combined, and look up what `Array.prototype.some` returns for different arrays.

Last, read `middleware.ts` and note exactly how a path is compared with the public routes list.

excerpts.quote: Two contain *real, finished algorithms* worth studying line by line

notes.title: Why customer.purge slips past approval
notes.body:
`requiresApproval` returns `command.includes("delete") || targetCount > 100`. The key "customer.purge" contains no "delete", and 50 is not above 100, so both conditions are false and no approval is needed. This is the loophole the chapter describes: the policy depends on how commands are named, not on how dangerous they are.

- *Every customer.* command*: the policy never looks at the namespace.
- *Purge listed as dangerous*: there is no list of verbs; only the substring "delete" is checked.
- *dangerLevel is low*: the function does not read dangerLevel at all.

notes.title: Why exactly 100 targets need no approval
notes.body:
The bulk condition is `targetCount > 100`, a strict comparison, so 100 is not enough; 101 would be. "billing.refund" does not contain "delete", so the whole expression is false.

- *>= 100*: the operator in the code is >, not >=.
- *Every refund needs approval*: refunds are not special-cased.
- *Refunds are never approved*: a refund to 101 customers would require approval.

notes.title: Why getCommand finds nothing today
notes.body:
The registry is a module-level `Map` that starts empty. Only `registerCommand` adds entries, and no file in `src` or `worker` calls it; the sixteen command files define objects but never register them. `getCommand` is `registry.get(key)`, which returns `undefined` for a missing key. Chapter 7 notes this and asks callers to handle the miss.

- *Registered on import*: importing a command file does not touch the registry.
- *Default no-op command*: there is no default.
- *Throws Unknown command*: Map.get never throws.

notes.title: Why no targeting rules means nobody
notes.body:
For a targeted flag, `evaluateFlag` returns `flag.targetingRules.some(...)`. `some` on an empty array returns false because no element satisfies the callback, so the flag is off for everyone. Chapter 8 lists this as a likely surprise for anyone who assumed "no rules" means "no restrictions".

- *Everybody*: that would need .every(), which is true for an empty array.
- *Default plan and region*: there are no defaults in the evaluator.
- *rolloutPercentage*: only the percentage type reads it.

notes.title: Why one matching rule is enough
notes.body:
`.some()` stops at the first rule whose callback returns true. The first rule `{ plan: "enterprise" }` fails because the customer is on pro. The second rule `{ region: "eu-west" }` specifies only a region, which matches, so its callback returns true and so does evaluateFlag.

- *Not on enterprise*: that only fails the first rule.
- *Both rules together*: rules are ORed; only conditions inside one rule are ANDed.
- *Percentage bucket*: targeted flags never compute a bucket.

notes.title: Why one mismatched condition fails the rule
notes.body:
Inside the callback each specified condition is checked with an early `return false`. The plan check passes (pro equals pro), then the region check sees "us-east" against "eu-west" and returns false. With only one rule, `.some()` returns false.

- *Plan is enough*: every specified condition must hold.
- *Region ignored when plan is present*: each condition is checked independently.
- *Plan rules only for enterprise*: the plan value is compared, whatever it is.

notes.title: Why a disabled flag is always off
notes.body:
The first guard clause in `evaluateFlag` is `if (!flag.isEnabled) return false`. It runs before the type is examined, so a disabled flag of any type returns false for every customer. The boolean branch `return true` is reached only for enabled flags.

- *Boolean flags are always on*: only when enabled.
- *Customer bucket*: buckets are only for percentage flags.
- *Targeting rules*: rules are only for targeted flags, and the guard runs first anyway.

notes.title: Why a 0% rollout reaches nobody
notes.body:
`hashToBucket` returns `Math.abs(hash % 100)`, so a bucket is a whole number from 0 to 99. The percentage branch returns `bucket < flag.rolloutPercentage`. With 0, no bucket is less than 0, so the flag is off for everyone; with 100, every bucket is less than 100.

- *About 1%*: bucket 0 is not less than 0.
- *All of them*: 0 is compared as a number, not read as "no limit".
- *Only bucket 0*: the comparison is strict.

notes.title: Why exactly 50% is sev2
notes.body:
`classifySeverity` checks `errorRate > 0.5`, then `> 0.2`, then `> 0.08`, all strict. At 0.5 the first test is false and the second is true, so the result is sev2. The order matters too: checking the lowest threshold first would classify almost everything as sev3.

- *sev1*: needs a rate above 0.5.
- *sev3*: 0.5 already passes the sev2 test.
- *sev4*: only rates at or below 0.08 fall through.

notes.title: Why an unknown role gets no permission
notes.body:
`hasPermission` evaluates `rolePermissions[role]?.includes(permission) ?? false`. For "auditor" the lookup is undefined, the optional chain short-circuits to undefined, and `?? false` turns it into false. Chapter 4 calls this deny by default: unknown roles get nothing.

- *Every role may read audit logs*: viewer, for example, has no audit.read.
- *Throws*: the optional chain prevents the TypeError.
- *Inherits viewer*: there is no fallback role.

notes.title: Which role can edit customers but not run operations
notes.body:
In `rolePermissions`, support has dashboard.read, customers.read, customers.write, incidents.manage and audit.read: customer writes, but no operations.execute. Support staff can fix customer records and manage incidents, but firing a dangerous operation is left to the ops roles. Reading the table as a grid makes questions like this quick to answer.

- *viewer*: only dashboard.read and customers.read, so no writes at all.
- *finance*: billing.manage and the read permissions, but no customers.write.
- *ops_engineer*: has customers.write and also operations.execute.

notes.title: Why /login-history counts as public
notes.body:
The middleware computes `isPublic = publicRoutes.some((route) => pathname.startsWith(route))` with publicRoutes `["/login", "/api/auth"]`. "/login-history" starts with "/login", so it is public, the auth check is skipped and `NextResponse.next()` runs. The prefix match is meant for `/api/auth/...` sub-paths, but it also opens any future route whose name begins with /login. Matching on path segments would avoid that.

- *Redirect to login*: that happens only for non-public paths.
- *401 envelope*: the middleware redirects; it never returns an API envelope.
- *GET only*: the method is not checked.

notes.title: How the login redirect remembers the page
notes.body:
For a non-public path without a session, the middleware builds `new URL("/login", req.url)`, calls `searchParams.set("next", pathname)` with the original path, and returns `NextResponse.redirect(loginUrl)` with an `x-request-id` header. After signing in, the login page can send the user back to /customers/cus_001.

- *No record of the page*: the next parameter carries it.
- *To / first*: the redirect goes straight to /login.
- *Page renders its own form*: the middleware runs before the page.
